units.text: Take the line y equals x, from zero to one. Square every height, and it sags. Higher powers sag further. Each curve is unbroken, from zero up to one. Pin one point, x equals nine tenths. Its heights go point nine, point eight one, point seven two nine, down toward zero. At x equals one, nothing moves. One to any power is one. So what shape are the curves heading for?

Flat at zero all the way to one, then a single point at height one. Unbroken curves, and a limit that jumps. A picture of a few curves can't prove that. Arithmetic can. Below one, each new power multiplies the height by the same number less than one.

Now let the point move. On each curve, mark where it crosses half height. There the curve is at one half and the limit is zero. As the power grows, the crossing creeps toward one, but the gap stays one half. So it matters who picks the point. Fix it first, and the gap shrinks to zero. Let it move with the curve, and the gap never does.

Shade every x where the curve is still above one half. That's a strip from the crossing up to one, and x equals one belongs to it. But at one, the curve and the limit are both at height one. The gap there is zero. So the gap is at least one half only on a strip that starts at the crossing and stops just short of one.
As the power grows, that strip gets narrower. Once it's thinner than a pixel, is the trouble gone?

No. Stretch the end of the interval sideways, ten times, a hundred times, a thousand times. The strip is still there. Reset the window to x to the tenth. Raise the power tenfold and stretch tenfold, then again. It looks almost the same. Its width shrinks like point six nine over n, and the strip is never empty. And the moving point is always inside it, with its gap of one half. A picture shows a few powers, at finite resolution. What we need is a guarantee for every point at once, and an order for who chooses what.

The guarantee has to answer an old objection. In seventeen thirty four, George Berkeley questioned a step in an argument for how fast a power changes. Here is that kind of argument for a square, in modern notation. Move x from one half by h, not zero. The height changes by h plus h squared. Divide by h, and the slope is one plus h.

Then the argument lets h vanish, so one plus h becomes one. Berkeley objected that h was something for the division and nothing afterward, yet the result was kept. So what slope does h equal to zero give?

None. Both points are then the same point, and the change is zero over zero. One is still the right answer, reached without h ever being zero. Shrink h from both sides, and the slopes close in on one. For every h within one tenth of zero, other than zero, the slope is within one tenth of one. Any tolerance works the same way, so the limit is one. This never needs the step Berkeley questioned. Who picks the tolerance, and when, comes next. Whether a limit exists at all is a separate question, for the end.

Make it a game with strict turns. The challenger names a tolerance, epsilon. The defender answers with a window, delta. Then the challenger picks any h in it but zero. Against one tenth, the defender answers one tenth. Every h the challenger can pick lands in the band, since each slope is as far from one as h is from zero. Catching some h is not enough. Answer one fifth instead, and point one five lands outside.

A limit leaves zero out. Continuity puts zero in and aims at the value there. Fill the hole with one, and it is continuous. Fill it with one and a half, and no window works. But if the defender could see h first, could this broken graph still win?

Yes, always, with a window too narrow to hold it. So the window may depend on the tolerance, the point and the curve, never on the later h. Continuity at x equals one, where the square's domain ends. Against one half, the window starts where x squared is one half, and every x from there to one passes. A winning answer covers every input in its window. Finding them is a search that written proofs hide.

A finished proof opens with a choice like delta equals two thirds of epsilon, and never says where it came from. Here is the search. Start from what the challenger demands. x squared must be within epsilon of a quarter, for every x near one half. That gap is the distance from one half, times x plus one half.

On the domain, zero to one, x plus one half is never more than three halves. That is the deliberate, generous step. So a distance below two thirds of epsilon is enough. That is where delta came from. Against one tenth, about how large could delta be, and still work?

About point zero nine two, where the curve leaves the band. One fifteenth is smaller, and still enough. A window only has to work for every input, not be the widest. Now read the proof forward, as it is written. Given epsilon, take delta as two thirds of epsilon. For every x in the domain and in the window, the gap is below three halves of delta, which is epsilon. The search ran backward from the goal. The proof runs forward, and hides it. Next, ways to make that search systematic.
